title: Judges 19:1–10
context: Judges 19 opens the last and darkest story of the book with the refrain that there was no king in Israel, a line that also frames chapters 17–18 and returns at 21:25. A Levite from the hill country of Ephraim takes a concubine from Bethlehem Judah; she leaves him and returns to her father’s house, and after four months he goes to bring her back. Her father’s repeated hospitality delays the journey until the Levite insists on leaving late in the day. The Hebrew text says she played the prostitute against him, while some ancient Greek and Latin witnesses say instead that she became angry with him, and interpreters weigh these readings differently. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the whole account as a narrative of moral collapse that the narrator reports rather than approves, and shared ground dominates their reading.

verses.text: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, there was a certain Levite living on the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim, who took for himself a concubine out of Bethlehem Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the story begins with the refrain that there was no king in Israel, signaling that what follows reflects a time of moral confusion. The Levite, who should have served God’s worship, is introduced in a troubled domestic situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the refrain as the narrator’s framing of these chapters as a portrait of a people without faithful leadership (compare 17:6; 18:1). Both traditions commonly read the opening as preparing readers for a story of collapse, not a model to follow.

verses.text: His concubine played the prostitute against him, and went away from him to her father’s house to Bethlehem Judah, and was there for four months.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Hebrew text says she played the prostitute against him, while some ancient Greek and Latin witnesses say she became angry with him. Either way, the marriage is broken and she returns to her father’s house for four months.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise weigh the textual difference with care, since it affects how readers understand her departure. Readers in both traditions commonly avoid building on either reading, noting that nothing in the text justifies what is later done to her.

verses.text: Her husband arose and went after her to speak kindly to her, to bring her again, having his servant with him and a couple of donkeys. She brought him into her father’s house; and when the father of the young lady saw him, he rejoiced to meet him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite going to speak kindly to her and bring her back, an action that could have led to reconciliation. The text says the father rejoiced to meet him, though it tells us little of the woman’s own view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the hopeful note in this verse, set against the grim outcome that follows. Both traditions commonly observe that the woman’s voice is never heard in the story, which invites readers to attend carefully to her dignity.

verses.text: His father-in-law, the young lady’s father, kept him there; and he stayed with him three days. So they ate and drank, and stayed there.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the father-in-law’s generous hospitality, keeping the Levite three days with food and drink. The warmth of this household contrasts sharply with the cold reception later in Gibeah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the contrast between hospitality in Bethlehem and its absence in Gibeah. Readers in both traditions commonly see the repeated delays as building tension in the narrative.

verses.text: On the fourth day, they got up early in the morning, and he rose up to depart. The young lady’s father said to his son-in-law, “Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread, and afterward you shall go your way.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the father’s urging to strengthen the heart with bread before leaving, an ordinary gesture of care. The narrative slows deliberately, drawing readers into the domestic scene.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detailed account of meals and delays as part of the narrator’s careful pacing. Both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the late departure that exposes the travelers to danger.

verses.text: So they sat down, ate, and drank, both of them together. Then the young lady’s father said to the man, “Please be pleased to stay all night, and let your heart be merry.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the father urging the Levite to stay another night and let his heart be merry. Hospitality here is generous, even insistent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the two men eat and drink together while the woman is not mentioned. Readers in both traditions commonly notice how the story centers on the men while the woman’s situation remains in the background.

verses.text: The man rose up to depart; but his father-in-law urged him, and he stayed there again.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Levite again tries to leave but stays when urged. The repeated pattern underscores the delay that will shape what follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator emphasizing the father-in-law’s persistent hospitality. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a deliberate contrast with the hostility the travelers will meet later.

verses.text: He arose early in the morning on the fifth day to depart; and the young lady’s father said, “Please strengthen your heart and stay until the day declines;” and they both ate.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the fifth day following the same pattern, with the father asking him to stay until the day declines. The repetition heightens the sense that time is slipping away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the repetition as building suspense. Readers in both traditions commonly see no doctrinal weight in these details beyond their role in the narrative.

verses.text: When the man rose up to depart, he, and his concubine, and his servant, his father-in-law, the young lady’s father, said to him, “Behold, now the day draws toward evening, please stay all night. Behold, the day is ending. Stay here, that your heart may be merry; and tomorrow go on your way early, that you may go home.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the father’s warning that the day is ending and his invitation to leave early the next day. Wise counsel is offered and declined.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the father-in-law’s plea as reasonable concern for the travelers’ safety. Both traditions commonly read the Levite’s refusal as a decision that exposes his household to danger.

verses.text: But the man wouldn’t stay that night, but he rose up and went near Jebus (also called Jerusalem). With him were a couple of saddled donkeys. His concubine also was with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite insisting on leaving that night and traveling near Jebus, which the text identifies as Jerusalem. His concubine is with him, but her wishes are not recorded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jebus was not yet an Israelite city at this point in the story (compare 19:12). Readers in both traditions commonly see the departure as the turning point toward the tragedy ahead.
